claims.text: Chemical short-range order plays a crucial role in governing the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Precipitation plays a crucial role in governing the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Ab-initio molecular dynamics simulations predict enhanced stability from formation of a stable precipitate phase.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloy is a random solid solution.
Thermal treatment or alloy design can introduce chemical short-range order.
Thermal treatment or alloy design can introduce precipitation.
Grain boundaries and precipitate phases mediate high-temperature stability.
Atomic-scale rearrangement and diffusion lead to formation of a stable precipitate phase.
Formation of a stable precipitate phase enhances the alloy's structural and chemical stability.
Introducing chemical short-range order and precipitation will reduce grain growth relative to a random solid-solution alloy without these features.
Introducing chemical short-range order and precipitation will improve thermal resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
Introducing chemical short-range order and precipitation will increase mechanical strength relative to the baseline alloy.
The prediction applies from 500°C to 1000°C over exposure times ranging from hours to days.
The prediction applies to quaternary or quinary high-entropy alloys.
A lack of significant differences in grain growth, thermal resistance, and mechanical strength between treated and untreated alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
